pos: v. and a. (condemned; the Authorized Version's word for the sentence of God upon unbelief, and upon the man who acts against his own conscience)
etymology: From Latin damnare, to condemn or inflict loss, from damnum, damage or penalty, through Old French damner. In 1611 the word was simply the legal term for a condemning verdict; its use as an oath came later and has largely destroyed it for ordinary speech.
biblical_def: The Authorized Version uses damned where a modern version says condemned, and the underlying Greek is katakrino — to give judgment against. Our Lord sets it opposite salvation: “He that believeth and is baptized shall be saved; but he that believeth not shall be damned” (Mark 16:16). Note precisely what is opposed to belief in the second clause: not the absence of baptism but the absence of faith. Paul states the ground of the same sentence at the end of the age: “That they all might be damned who believed not the truth, but had pleasure in unrighteousness” (2 Thessalonians 2:12) — unbelief and pleasure in unrighteousness together, the will as much as the mind. Then Paul uses the word in a much narrower and more searching way, of a Christian brother at table: “And he that doubteth is damned if he eat, because he eateth not of faith: for whatsoever is not of faith is sin” (Romans 14:23). Here the condemnation is of a particular act, not of the person, and the principle drawn out of it is one of the great rules of the Christian conscience: an act done against a doubting conscience is sin even when the thing itself is lawful.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines damn as to condemn, to doom to punishment in the future world, and notes the word's proper use is judicial.
webster_full: DAMNED, pp. Condemned; sentenced to everlasting punishment.
DAMN, v.t. To condemn.
2. To doom to punishment in a future state; to punish eternally.
3. To condemn; to decide to be wrong or worthy of punishment.
DAMNATION, n. Condemnation; sentence or judgment which condemns.
scriptures: Mark 16:16
He that believeth and is baptized shall be saved; but he that believeth not shall be damned.
2 Thessalonians 2:12
That they all might be damned who believed not the truth, but had pleasure in unrighteousness.
Romans 14:23
And he that doubteth is damned if he eat, because he eateth not of faith: for whatsoever is not of faith is sin.
1 Corinthians 11:29
For he that eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh damnation to himself, not discerning the Lord's body.
corruption_summary: Profanity has worn the word out for judicial use, and universalism has emptied it of content — both leaving the doctrine unsayable.
corruption_paragraphs: Two forces have taken this word from the church. The first is profanity: after three centuries as an oath, damned can scarcely be spoken from a pulpit without a snicker, and preachers reach for condemned to be heard at all. That is a reasonable accommodation, provided nothing is lost with the word. The second force intends the loss. Universalism — whether the older Origenist form, the modern larger hope, or the popular evangelical version that hopes everyone is finally in — empties the sentence of any content, so that Mark 16:16 becomes a warning about nothing. Scripture will not have it. The two halves of that verse are set in exact opposition, and the second is as real as the first.

Romans 14:23 preserves the word's narrower use and it should not be lost either. A man who eats while doubting whether he may is condemned in that act, though the food was lawful and his brother eats it freely. Paul's conclusion — whatsoever is not of faith is sin — is one of the most practically useful sentences in the epistle, and it cuts in both directions: it forbids the strong brother to press the weak past his conscience, and it forbids the weak brother to make his conscience a rule for the church. Where the doctrine of divine judgment is soft, this pastoral use goes soft with it, and Christian liberty degenerates into indifference.
roots_summary: Greek katakrino, to give judgment against — Mark 16:16, Romans 14:23; krima, a sentence or judgment — 1 Corinthians 11:29; Latin damnare, to condemn.
roots_lines: Greek katakrino — to judge against, to condemn; Mark 16:16 and Romans 14:23.
Greek krino — to judge; the simple verb from which the compound is formed.
Greek krima — the sentence rendered; 1 Corinthians 11:29, rendered damnation.
Greek apoleia — destruction, perdition; the outcome of the sentence in 2 Thessalonians 2.
Latin damnum, loss or penalty, whence damnare — the word was purely judicial in 1611.
usage: “He that believeth not shall be damned” — unbelief, not the absence of the ordinance, is the ground.
“He that doubteth is damned if he eat” — a lawful act done against conscience is sin.
“Whatsoever is not of faith is sin” — the rule Paul draws from it.

pos: a. (containing impious speech against God or holy things; the charge laid falsely against Stephen and truly against the beast)
etymology: From Greek blasphemos, from blapto, to injure, and pheme, speech — injurious speech. The word came into Latin and thence English unchanged in sense; the English blame descends from the same Greek root by a different road.
biblical_def: The Authorized Version's two occurrences of the adjective both fall in the trial of Stephen, and both are lies. “Then they suborned men, which said, We have heard him speak blasphemous words against Moses, and against God” (Acts 6:11); and again, “And set up false witnesses, which said, This man ceaseth not to speak blasphemous words against this holy place, and the law” (Acts 6:13). Luke tells the reader in advance that the men were suborned and the witnesses false, so that the charge is exposed before it is heard — and the same charge had been brought against Stephen's Master. Blasphemy is real, and Scripture treats it with the utmost gravity: “All manner of sin and blasphemy shall be forgiven unto men: but the blasphemy against the Holy Ghost shall not be forgiven unto men” (Matthew 12:31). At the end, the beast is given “a mouth speaking great things and blasphemies” (Revelation 13:5). Two things therefore stand together in the New Testament: blasphemy is a genuine and terrible sin, and the accusation of blasphemy is one of the standard weapons used against faithful men. The one truth does not excuse the abuse of the other.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines blasphemous as containing blasphemy, impiously irreverent or reproachful toward God.
webster_full: BLASPHEMOUS, a. Containing blasphemy; calumnious; impiously irreverent or reproachful towards God.
BLASPHEMY, n. An indignity offered to God by words or writing; reproachful, contemptuous or irreverent words uttered impiously against Jehovah.
2. That which derogates from the prerogatives of God.
BLASPHEME, v.t. To speak of the Supreme Being in terms of impious irreverence; to revile or speak reproachfully of God.
2. To speak evil of; to utter abuse or calumny against; to speak reproachfully of.
scriptures: Acts 6:11
Then they suborned men, which said, We have heard him speak blasphemous words against Moses, and against God.
Acts 6:13
And set up false witnesses, which said, This man ceaseth not to speak blasphemous words against this holy place, and the law:
Matthew 12:31
Wherefore I say unto you, All manner of sin and blasphemy shall be forgiven unto men: but the blasphemy against the Holy Ghost shall not be forgiven unto men.
Revelation 13:5
And there was given unto him a mouth speaking great things and blasphemies; and power was given unto him to continue forty and two months.
corruption_summary: Blasphemy is treated as an obsolete superstition, while the accusation itself survives — transferred to whatever the age holds sacred.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern secular claim is that blasphemy is a category no free society should recognise, since it protects an idea from criticism. What has actually happened is not the abolition of the category but its transfer. Every society enforces a boundary around what may not be reviled; the change is in what stands inside the boundary. Speech against the true God is now unremarkable, and speech against the current sacred causes is punished by loss of employment and reputation with a thoroughness the old ecclesiastical courts rarely managed. The category was never going to disappear, because men are worshipping creatures. The only question is what is being protected.

Acts 6 requires the church to hold two things at once. Blasphemy is real, and Matthew 12:31 shows how gravely our Lord regarded it. And the charge of blasphemy is a standard instrument against faithful preaching — laid against Christ, against Stephen, and against a long line since. Luke's deliberate note that the witnesses were suborned and false is the safeguard. Where a man is accused of speaking against the holy place, the first question is not how loudly he is accused but whether the accusation is true, and the answer is found in Scripture rather than in the volume of the crowd.
roots_summary: Greek blasphemos, speaking injuriously — Acts 6:11, 13; blasphemia, blasphemy — Matthew 12:31, Revelation 13:5; from blapto, to harm, and pheme, speech.
roots_lines: Greek blasphemos — injurious in speech, blasphemous; Acts 6:11 and 6:13, in the mouths of false witnesses.
Greek blasphemia — the noun; Matthew 12:31 and Revelation 13:5.
Greek blapto — to injure, and pheme, report or speech; the two elements of the compound.
Hebrew naqab — to pierce, to curse the Name; Leviticus 24:16, the Old Testament statute.
Hebrew gadaph — to revile, to blaspheme; 2 Kings 19:6 of Rabshakeh's words.
usage: “They suborned men” — Luke exposes the charge before he records it.
“The blasphemy against the Holy Ghost shall not be forgiven” — the sin is real and grave.
“A mouth speaking great things and blasphemies” — the beast's characteristic organ.

pos: v. (boasts, exults; the archaic third person of glory, and the hinge of Jeremiah's rule that Paul quotes twice)
etymology: From Latin gloriari, to boast, from gloria, glory, through Old French. The Authorized Version's -eth ending is the ordinary third-person singular of 1611. The Hebrew at Jeremiah 9:24 is halal, to praise or boast; the Greek at 1 Corinthians 1:31 is kauchaomai.
biblical_def: Jeremiah lays down a rule that governs the whole doctrine of boasting: “Thus saith the LORD, Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, let not the rich man glory in his riches” (Jeremiah 9:23) — and then, rather than forbidding boasting altogether, redirects it: “But let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me, that I am the LORD which exercise lovingkindness, judgment, and righteousness, in the earth: for in these things I delight, saith the LORD” (Jeremiah 9:24). Three grounds of pride are named — wisdom, might, riches — and each is a thing men actually possess; the objection is not that the boast is false but that the ground is wrong. Paul quotes the rule twice, and both times as the conclusion of an argument about the humbling of human pride: “He that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 1:31; 2 Corinthians 10:17). In the first he has just said that God chose the foolish, the weak, and the base things of the world, that no flesh should glory in his presence. The doctrines of election and of grace alone are not abstractions; they exist in Scripture in this practical form, to put an end to boasting.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives glory as a verb meaning to boast, to be proud of, and notes that in a good sense it is to rejoice or exult in what is right.
webster_full: GLORY, v.i. To boast; to be proud of; to be vain of; to exult with joy.
No one should glory in his prosperity.
2. To rejoice; to be proud of, with a good sense; as, to glory in the cross of Christ.
GLORYING, n. Boasting; a boast or vaunt.
GLORY, n. Praise ascribed in adoration; honor and admiration.
scriptures: Jeremiah 9:24

But let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me, that I am the LORD which exercise lovingkindness, judgment, and righteousness, in the earth: for in these things I delight, saith the LORD.
Jeremiah 9:23
Thus saith the LORD, Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, let not the rich man glory in his riches:
1 Corinthians 1:31
That, according as it is written, He that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord.
2 Corinthians 10:17
But he that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord.
corruption_summary: The rule is read as a ban on all confidence, or ignored entirely in a ministry culture built on visible achievement.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah 9:23-24 is misread in both directions. Some take it as forbidding any satisfaction in any thing, producing a false humility that cannot receive a gift or acknowledge a mercy — which is not the text, since the LORD does not abolish the boast but assigns it an object. Others quote the verse and then build ministries on precisely the three grounds it names. Wisdom, might, and riches are the currencies of contemporary religious influence as surely as they were of Jerusalem's, and a movement can affirm sola gratia in its statement of faith while running entirely on platform, reach, and budget.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the corruption is the perennial one of the human heart. The principle to recover is the object. What a man glories in reveals what he trusts, and Jeremiah names the permitted ground with great precision — not that I am saved, and not that I am right, but that he understandeth and knoweth me, and specifically knows the LORD as one who exercises lovingkindness, judgment, and righteousness in the earth. That is a boast in God's character, made by a man who has been given to know it. Paul's use in 1 Corinthians 1 ties it directly to election: God chose as He did so that no flesh should glory in His presence.
roots_summary: Hebrew halal, to praise or boast — Jeremiah 9:23-24; Greek kauchaomai, to boast — 1 Corinthians 1:31, 2 Corinthians 10:17; Latin gloriari, to boast.
roots_lines: Hebrew halal — to shine, to praise, to boast; the root also of hallelujah. Jeremiah 9:23-24.
Greek kauchaomai — to boast or exult; 1 Corinthians 1:31 and 2 Corinthians 10:17, both quoting Jeremiah.
Greek kauchema — the ground of boasting; Romans 4:2, where Abraham has none before God.
Latin gloriari, from gloria — the source of the English verb.
The -eth ending is simply the 1611 third person singular, as doeth, saith, knoweth.
usage: “Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom” — three real possessions, three wrong grounds.
“He that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord” — Paul quotes the rule twice.
“That no flesh should glory in his presence” — the pastoral point of election.

pos: v. (builds up; the archaic third person of edify, and Paul's test for everything said in the assembly)
etymology: From Latin aedificare, to build a house, from aedes, a building, and facere, to make — through Old French edifier. The Greek is oikodomeo, formed the same way from oikos, a house, and demo, to build. Both languages make edification an architectural word.
biblical_def: Paul's governing image for the church is a building under construction, and edify is the builder's verb. He sets it against mere knowledge: “Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth” (1 Corinthians 8:1). The contrast is exact — one word means to inflate and the other to build; the first enlarges a man's opinion of himself, the second raises a structure that will stand. In the great chapter on tongues and prophecy he applies the same test to public worship: “He that speaketh in an unknown tongue edifieth himself; but he that prophesieth edifieth the church” (1 Corinthians 14:4). Paul does not deny that the first man is edified; he denies that it is enough, because the assembly exists for the building of the whole body. The chapter closes with the rule stated bare: “Let all things be done unto edifying” (1 Corinthians 14:26). Ephesians extends it from public speech to every word a believer utters: “Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers” (Ephesians 4:29). Speech is either building or demolition; there is no neutral ground.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines edify as to build in a moral and religious sense, to instruct and improve the mind in knowledge and the heart in holiness.
webster_full: EDIFY, v.t. To build, in a moral and religious sense; to instruct and improve the mind in knowledge generally, and particularly in moral and religious knowledge, in faith and holiness.
Edify one another. 1 Thess. 5:11.
2. To teach or persuade.
EDIFICATION, n. Improvement and progress of the mind, in knowledge, in morals, or in faith and holiness.
EDIFICE, n. A building; a structure; a fabric; but chiefly applied to elegant houses and other large structures.
scriptures: 1 Corinthians 8:1
Now as touching things offered unto idols, we know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth.
1 Corinthians 14:4
He that speaketh in an unknown tongue edifieth himself; but he that prophesieth edifieth the church.
1 Corinthians 14:26
How is it then, brethren? when ye come together, every one of you hath a psalm, hath a doctrine, hath a tongue, hath a revelation, hath an interpretation. Let all things be done unto edifying.
Ephesians 4:29
Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers.
corruption_summary: Edification has been redefined as whatever leaves the hearer feeling encouraged, so that a sermon is judged by the mood it produces.
corruption_paragraphs: The common modern equation is that edifying means uplifting — a message is edifying if it sends people out lighter than they came. Paul's word is architectural, not emotional. To edify is to build, and building involves excavation, the setting of load-bearing members, and the removal of what will not hold weight. Ephesians 4:29 is often quoted to silence any hard word, but read it: the standard is good to the use of edifying, and rebuke is one of the most edifying things a man can receive. The same apostle who wrote that verse wrote 1 Corinthians 5. A ministry that never says a difficult thing is not building; it is decorating.

The opposite error is equally live in Reformed circles, and Paul addresses it first. Knowledge puffeth up was written to men who were doctrinally correct about idol-meat and were destroying weaker brethren with their correctness. Being right is not the same as building, and a congregation can be well taught and unedified at once. The test in 1 Corinthians 14 is not the speaker's soundness but the hearers' construction: does the whole body rise? That test cuts through both the sentimental and the merely accurate ministry, and it is the reason Paul preferred five words with understanding to ten thousand in an unknown tongue.
roots_summary: Greek oikodomeo, to build a house — 1 Corinthians 8:1, 14:4; oikodome, the building or the act of building — Ephesians 4:29; phusioo, to inflate — the contrast in 1 Corinthians 8:1.
roots_lines: Greek oikodomeo — to build a house, from oikos and demo; 1 Corinthians 8:1 and 14:4.
Greek oikodome — the building itself, and the act of building; Ephesians 4:29 and 1 Corinthians 14:26.
Greek phusioo — to puff up, to inflate with air; the deliberate contrast at 1 Corinthians 8:1.
Greek agape — charity, love; the thing that builds where knowledge only swells.
Latin aedificare, from aedes, a building — the source of English edify and edifice.
usage: “Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth” — inflation against construction.
“Let all things be done unto edifying” — the rule for the whole assembly.
“Good to the use of edifying” — the test for every word out of a believer's mouth.

pos: n. (a recommending; in the New Testament chiefly the letters of introduction that vouched for a travelling Christian, and the self-commendation Paul refuses)
etymology: From Latin commendare, to entrust or commit to the care of another, from com- and mandare, to commit. The Greek is sustatikos, from sunistemi, to place together, to introduce or vouch for.
biblical_def: The word occurs once in the Authorized Version, and it names a real institution of the apostolic churches: “Do we begin again to commend ourselves? or need we, as some others, epistles of commendation to you, or letters of commendation from you?” (2 Corinthians 3:1). Travelling Christians carried letters vouching for them, because a stranger claiming to be a brother could not otherwise be received; Paul's own commendation of Phebe is such a letter embedded in an epistle — “I commend unto you Phebe our sister, which is a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea” (Romans 16:1). Paul's point in 2 Corinthians is that the Corinthians themselves are his letter, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God. Behind the argument stands his rule about the whole business: “For not he that commendeth himself is approved, but whom the Lord commendeth” (2 Corinthians 10:18). And there is a right self-commending, which he also states: “by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man's conscience in the sight of God” (2 Corinthians 4:2). A man commends himself rightly by open truth-telling that the hearer's own conscience can weigh, and wrongly by the recommendation he writes for himself.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines commendation as the act of commending, praise, favorable representation in words, and also a message of love or respect.
webster_full: COMMENDATION, n. The act of commending; praise; favorable representation in words; declaration of esteem.
Need we, as some others, epistles of commendation to you? 2 Cor. 3.
2. Ground of esteem, approbation or praise.
3. Service; respects; message of love.
COMMEND, v.t. To represent as worthy of notice, regard, or kindness; to speak well of; to praise.
scriptures: 2 Corinthians 3:1
Do we begin again to commend ourselves? or need we, as some others, epistles of commendation to you, or letters of commendation from you?
2 Corinthians 10:18
For not he that commendeth himself is approved, but whom the Lord commendeth.
2 Corinthians 4:2

But have renounced the hidden things of dishonesty, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully; but by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man's conscience in the sight of God.
Romans 16:1
I commend unto you Phebe our sister, which is a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea:
corruption_summary: Commendation has been replaced by platform metrics, so that a teacher is received on the strength of his following rather than a church's testimony.
corruption_paragraphs: The apostolic churches had a plain answer to the question of who may be received and heard: a letter from a congregation that knew the man. It was slow, personal, and accountable, and it tied a teacher to a body of believers who could vouch for his life as well as his doctrine. The modern equivalent is a follower count. A man is received because he is known, and he is known because he is visible, and he is visible because he was effective at becoming so — a chain with no point in it at which anyone who has watched his household attests to his character. 2 Corinthians 10:18 speaks directly to the arrangement: not he that commendeth himself is approved.

The corrective is not to distrust every teacher who is widely heard, which would be its own foolishness, but to restore the local anchoring the letters provided. Paul, who refused to trade in self-commendation, wrote commendations freely for others — Phebe, Timothy, Epaphroditus — and was content to let the Corinthians themselves stand as his credential. 2 Corinthians 4:2 gives the manner of the only self-commending he allowed: renouncing hidden things, refusing craft, handling the word without deceit, and setting the plain truth before every man's conscience in the sight of God. A ministry conducted that way requires no letter and will survive without one.
roots_summary: Greek sustatikos, commendatory — 2 Corinthians 3:1; sunistemi, to place together, to commend — 2 Corinthians 4:2, 10:18, Romans 16:1; Latin commendare, to entrust.
roots_lines: Greek sustatikos — commendatory, of a letter of introduction; 2 Corinthians 3:1, its only occurrence.
Greek sunistemi — to set together, to introduce or prove; Romans 16:1 and 2 Corinthians 10:18.
Greek dokimos — approved after testing; the word behind approved in 2 Corinthians 10:18.
Greek epistole — a letter; the Corinthians themselves are Paul's, written by the Spirit.
Latin commendare, from mandare, to commit — a commendation entrusts a person to another's care.
usage: “Epistles of commendation” — the apostolic churches' means of receiving a stranger.
“Not he that commendeth himself is approved” — the rule over the whole practice.
“I commend unto you Phebe our sister” — a letter of commendation preserved in an epistle.

pos: n. pl. (salutations in public; three times in the Gospels of the deference the scribes and Pharisees loved to receive in the markets)
etymology: From Old English gretan, to approach or accost. The Greek is aspasmos, a salutation, from aspazomai, to embrace or salute — an ordinary courtesy word which becomes, in these three texts, an index of a corrupt heart.
biblical_def: All three occurrences in the Authorized Version are indictments, and they concern not the greeting but the love of it. In the woes our Lord itemises what the scribes and Pharisees desire: “And greetings in the markets, and to be called of men, Rabbi, Rabbi” (Matthew 23:7). Luke records the same charge twice: “Woe unto you, Pharisees! for ye love the uppermost seats in the synagogues, and greetings in the markets” (Luke 11:43); and “Beware of the scribes, which desire to walk in long robes, and love greetings in the markets, and the highest seats in the synagogues, and the chief rooms at feasts” (Luke 20:46). The pattern is consistent: a robe that marks a man out, a seat that ranks him, a public salutation that repeats the ranking in the street. None of these things is sinful in itself — a salutation is a courtesy, and the New Testament epistles are full of them. The sin is the appetite. Our Lord's remedy follows immediately in Matthew: “whosoever shall exalt himself shall be abased; and he that shall humble himself shall be exalted” (Matthew 23:12). The market greeting is the smallest and most ordinary of honours, which is precisely why loving it is so revealing.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a greeting as a salutation or compliment at meeting, or an expression of kindness sent by words or writing.
webster_full: GREETING, n. Salutation at meeting; compliment addressed from one absent.
GREET, v.t. To address with expressions of kind wishes; to salute.
2. To congratulate.
3. To pay compliments at a distance.
SALUTATION, n. The act of saluting; a greeting; the act of paying respect or reverence by the customary words or actions.
scriptures: Matthew 23:7
And greetings in the markets, and to be called of men, Rabbi, Rabbi.
Luke 11:43
Woe unto you, Pharisees! for ye love the uppermost seats in the synagogues, and greetings in the markets.
Luke 20:46
Beware of the scribes, which desire to walk in long robes, and love greetings in the markets, and the highest seats in the synagogues, and the chief rooms at feasts;
Matthew 23:12
And whosoever shall exalt himself shall be abased; and he that shall humble himself shall be exalted.
corruption_summary: The appetite our Lord exposed has simply migrated to the public feed, where the greeting in the market is now counted and displayed.
corruption_paragraphs: The market of Matthew 23:7 was the place a man was seen and acknowledged, and the scribes loved being greeted there because the greeting was public and it ranked them. The mechanism has not changed; only its scale has. A modern platform delivers the market greeting in measurable quantities, publishes the count beside the name, and adjusts a man's visibility according to how much of it he attracts. What was once an appetite a Pharisee had to walk to the market to feed is now available continuously, and the men most exposed to it are frequently the men in ministry — which is exactly who our Lord was addressing.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the corruption is the ancient one, newly equipped. The principle to recover is the distinction our Lord assumes throughout the passage. He does not forbid greetings, robes, seats, or feasts; Paul ends his letters with long lists of salutations, and the church is told to greet one another. What is condemned is the loving of it — the state of a soul that needs the acknowledgment and arranges its life to receive more. Matthew 23:12 supplies the only real cure, and it is not a technique but a promise about who does the exalting.
roots_summary: Greek aspasmos, a salutation — Matthew 23:7, Luke 11:43, 20:46; aspazomai, to salute or embrace — the verb behind the epistolary greetings; phileo, to love — the verb of the appetite condemned.
roots_lines: Greek aspasmos — a salutation, greeting; Matthew 23:7 and the two Lukan parallels.
Greek aspazomai — to salute, embrace; the ordinary verb of the epistles' closing greetings.
Greek phileo — to love, to be fond of; Matthew 23:6-7, the verb that carries the sin.
Greek agora — the marketplace; the public place where a man was seen and ranked.
Old English gretan — to approach, accost; the source of the English word.
usage: “Greetings in the markets” — the smallest public honour, and the most revealing to love.
“To be called of men, Rabbi, Rabbi” — the title repeated, which is the point of it.
“Whosoever shall exalt himself shall be abased” — the promise that ends the appetite.

pos: interj. and n. (a parting word; literally may you fare well, and in the New Testament both a lawful courtesy and, once, an excuse for delay)
etymology: From the imperative fare — Old English faran, to travel or get on — with well: a wish that the departing person may journey and prosper. The Greek at 2 Corinthians 13:11 is chairo, rejoice, the ordinary Greek word of parting as well as of greeting.
biblical_def: The word appears in three quite different registers. First as a request that our Lord refuses: “And another also said, Lord, I will follow thee; but let me first go bid them farewell, which are at home at my house” (Luke 9:61). The request looks entirely reasonable — Elisha was permitted exactly this when Elijah called him — and our Lord's answer about the plough and the backward look is one of the hardest in the Gospels. The issue is the word first: a claim placed ahead of the call. Second as ordinary apostolic courtesy, in Paul's departure from Ephesus: “But bade them farewell, saying, I must by all means keep this feast that cometh in Jerusalem: but I will return again unto you, if God will” (Acts 18:21) — note the if God will, the standing qualification on every plan. Third as the closing word of an epistle, where it carries a weight the English disguises: “Finally, brethren, farewell. Be perfect, be of good comfort, be of one mind, live in peace; and the God of love and peace shall be with you” (2 Corinthians 13:11). The Greek is chairete, rejoice, so that Paul's last word to a difficult church is a command to joy, followed by four more commands and a promise.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) treats farewell as a compound of fare and well — go well, succeed, prosper — an expression of good wishes at parting.
webster_full: FAREWELL. Compounded of fare, in the imperative, and well. Go well; originally applied to a person departing, but by custom now applied both to those who depart and those who remain.
It expresses a kind wish, a wish of happiness to those who leave or those who stay.
FAREWELL, n. A wish of happiness or welfare at parting; the parting compliment; adieu.
2. Leave; act of departure.
FARE, v.i. To go; to pass; to move forward; to travel.
scriptures: Luke 9:61
And another also said, Lord, I will follow thee; but let me first go bid them farewell, which are at home at my house.
Acts 18:21
But bade them farewell, saying, I must by all means keep this feast that cometh in Jerusalem: but I will return again unto you, if God will. And he sailed from Ephesus.
2 Corinthians 13:11
Finally, brethren, farewell. Be perfect, be of good comfort, be of one mind, live in peace; and the God of love and peace shall be with you.
Acts 20:37
And they all wept sore, and fell on Paul's neck, and kissed him,
corruption_summary: Luke 9:61 is regularly softened into a general call to enthusiasm, when the point is the single word first.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke 9:61 makes readers uncomfortable, and the discomfort produces two evasions. One treats our Lord's answer as hyperbole not to be pressed, and the passage becomes a vague encouragement toward keenness. The other reads it as a general devaluing of family, which contradicts the fifth commandment and the whole tenor of Scripture. The text is more precise than either. The man says let me first, and the offence is in the ordering, not in the affection; he has placed a claim, and a reasonable one, ahead of the call of Christ. Elisha was given leave to kiss his father and mother, so the request is not sinful in itself. What may not be done is to file it before the summons.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond that softening. The principle to recover is the ordering of loves, which the whole Christian tradition has treated as the substance of holiness. Nothing in Luke 9 is condemned as evil — a burial, a farewell, a home; these are goods. Disordered goods are how most Christians are actually lost to usefulness, not by choosing wickedness but by choosing the lesser good first. Paul models the ordered version at Ephesus: he bids farewell, states his purpose, and attaches it to if God will.
roots_summary: Greek apotassomai, to take leave of — Luke 9:61; apotassomai again in Acts 18:21; chairo, rejoice, the Greek parting word — 2 Corinthians 13:11.
roots_lines: Greek apotassomai — to set apart from oneself, to take leave; Luke 9:61 and Acts 18:21.
Greek chairo — to rejoice; used at both meeting and parting, and rendered farewell at 2 Corinthians 13:11.
Greek proton — first; the single word that makes Luke 9:61 a refusal.
Old English faran — to travel, to get on; the imperative in the English compound.
Acts 18:21 attaches if God will to the plan, the standing New Testament qualification.
usage: “Let me first go bid them farewell” — the offence is first, not the farewell.
“I will return again unto you, if God will” — every plan under that clause.
Chairete: Paul's last word to Corinth is a command to rejoice.

pos: a. (exactly representing; in Hebrews 1:3, of the Son as the express image of the Father's person — the impression a seal leaves in wax)
etymology: From Latin exprimere, to press out, from ex and premere, to press — hence to form by pressure, and so to represent exactly. The Greek at Hebrews 1:3 is charakter, the engraved die or the impression it leaves; the English character is the same word.
biblical_def: The great occurrence is Christological: “Who being the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person, and upholding all things by the word of his power, when he had by himself purged our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high” (Hebrews 1:3). Two images stand together. Brightness renders apaugasma, the radiance streaming from a light source — not a reflection but the shining itself, of one substance with the light. Express image renders charakter, the exact impression left by an engraved die, so that the stamp carries every feature of the seal. The Son is not a copy, a lesser reproduction, or an emanation; He bears the exact impress of the Father's very substance. Paul says the same in another figure: “Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature” (Colossians 1:15). And our Lord Himself makes the claim plainly: “he that hath seen me hath seen the Father” (John 14:9). These texts stand behind the Nicene confession of one substance with the Father, and they are the reason the church has never allowed that the Son is merely the highest of creatures.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines express as copied, resembling, exactly representing — and cites the Hebrews text as its example.
webster_full: EXPRESS, a. Copied; resembling; bearing an exact representation.
His face express; Hebrews 1:3, the express image of his person.
2. Directly and distinctly stated; not merely implied; as an express command.
3. Given in direct terms; not ambiguous.
EXPRESS, v.t. To press or squeeze out; to force out by pressure.
scriptures: Hebrews 1:3

Who being the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person, and upholding all things by the word of his power, when he had by himself purged our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high;
Colossians 1:15
Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature:
John 14:9
Jesus saith unto him, Have I been so long time with you, and yet hast thou not known me, Philip? he that hath seen me hath seen the Father; and how sayest thou then, Shew us the Father?
John 1:18
No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him.
corruption_summary: Every subordinationist scheme — ancient Arian and modern — must weaken charakter into resemblance, and Hebrews 1:3 will not bear the weakening.
corruption_paragraphs: Arius taught that the Son was the first and highest of created beings, like the Father but not of the same substance, and the Council of Nicaea answered with homoousios. The argument turned on texts of exactly this kind. Charakter is not the language of resemblance; it is the language of an impression that carries every line of the die. A seal and its stamp are not two similar things but one form in two media. The same objection defeats the modern versions of the error — the Jehovah's Witnesses' created Son, the various liberal reductions of Christ to the supreme God-conscious man, and any scheme in which the Son is the Father's best representative rather than God of God.

Colossians 1:15 is the usual battleground, since firstborn of every creature is read as making Him a creature. The word prototokos denotes rank and right of inheritance rather than origin in time — David is called the firstborn though he was the eighth son — and the following verse settles it: by Him were all things created, which cannot be said of one of the things created. Hebrews 1:3 closes the matter by attributing to the Son the upholding of all things by the word of His power, and then the purging of sins, and then the session at the right hand of the Majesty. Creatures do not do those things.
roots_summary: Greek charakter, the engraved die and its impression — Hebrews 1:3; apaugasma, effulgence — the same verse; eikon, image — Colossians 1:15; Latin exprimere, to press out.
roots_lines: Greek charakter — the tool that engraves and the exact impression it leaves; Hebrews 1:3, its only New Testament occurrence.
Greek apaugasma — radiance streaming from its source; the companion word in the same verse.
Greek hupostasis — substance, the underlying reality; rendered person in Hebrews 1:3.
Greek eikon — image, likeness; Colossians 1:15, of the invisible God.
Latin exprimere, to press out — the source of the English word, and exactly the seal-and-wax picture.
usage: Charakter: the die and its impression — one form in two media, not two similar things.
“The brightness of his glory” — the shining itself, not a reflection of it.
“He that hath seen me hath seen the Father” — the same doctrine in our Lord's own words.

pos: v. and a. (prohibited by authority; of what the commandments forbid, and of the door the Holy Ghost shut against Paul in Asia)
etymology: From Old English forbeodan, to command against, from the prefix for-, expressing prohibition, and beodan, to bid. The Greek at Acts 16:6 is koluo, to hinder or prevent — the same verb used when our Lord forbids the disciples to hinder the children.
biblical_def: Two uses of the word run through Scripture, and they must be kept apart. The first is moral prohibition. “And if a soul sin, and commit any of these things which are forbidden to be done by the commandments of the LORD; though he wist it not, yet is he guilty, and shall bear his iniquity” (Leviticus 5:17). The clause though he wist it not is the striking one: ignorance of the prohibition does not dissolve the guilt, though the law provides a sacrifice for it — a standing rebuke to the notion that sin requires conscious intent. Moses applies the same to the second commandment: “make you a graven image, or the likeness of any thing, which the LORD thy God hath forbidden thee” (Deuteronomy 4:23). The second use is providential rather than moral: “Now when they had gone throughout Phrygia and the region of Galatia, and were forbidden of the Holy Ghost to preach the word in Asia” (Acts 16:6), followed by “they assayed to go into Bithynia: but the Spirit suffered them not” (Acts 16:7). Nothing sinful was proposed; preaching the word in Asia was a good thing, and Paul would later do it at length. The closed door was not a rebuke but a redirection, and it ended at Troas with the vision of the man of Macedonia.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines forbid as to prohibit, to interdict, to command not to do a thing, and also to oppose or hinder.
webster_full: FORBIDDEN, pp. Prohibited; interdicted; hindered; obstructed.
FORBID, v.t. To prohibit; to interdict; to command to forbear or not to do.
The laws of God forbid us to swear.
2. To command not to enter; to hinder; to restrain.
3. To oppose; to obstruct; to render impracticable.
scriptures: Leviticus 5:17
And if a soul sin, and commit any of these things which are forbidden to be done by the commandments of the LORD; though he wist it not, yet is he guilty, and shall bear his iniquity.
Deuteronomy 4:23

Take heed unto yourselves, lest ye forget the covenant of the LORD your God, which he made with you, and make you a graven image, or the likeness of any thing, which the LORD thy God hath forbidden thee.
Acts 16:6
Now when they had gone throughout Phrygia and the region of Galatia, and were forbidden of the Holy Ghost to preach the word in Asia,
Acts 16:7
After they were come to Mysia, they assayed to go into Bithynia: but the Spirit suffered them not.
corruption_summary: Sin is redefined as requiring conscious intent, so that Leviticus 5:17 becomes unintelligible and much of the law becomes optional.
corruption_paragraphs: The prevailing moral instinct is that a man is culpable only for what he meant. Leviticus 5:17 states the opposite plainly: he commits a forbidden thing, he wist it not, he is guilty, and he shall bear his iniquity. The Reformed doctrine of sins of ignorance follows from this text and from Psalm 19:12, who can understand his errors? cleanse thou me from secret faults. The point is not to make God arbitrary; it is that God's law defines sin, and a creature's awareness does not create or dissolve the standard. The gospel implication is enormous, since no man knows the full extent of his own guilt, and therefore no man can measure the atonement he needs. The law which convicts a man of what he did not know he did is the law that drives him to a Substitute.

The second use has its own live corruption, in the opposite direction. Acts 16 is regularly read as a template for reading providence as personal direction, so that any closed door becomes the Spirit's specific instruction and any open one a divine endorsement. Luke does not encourage the method. He records an apostolic band being hindered twice and then given an explicit vision, and he offers no technique for distinguishing the Spirit's restraint from ordinary difficulty. Paul, hindered from Asia, did not stop; he kept moving until the way opened. Obedience proceeds by the revealed will of God in Scripture, with providence read afterwards, not as a substitute for it.
roots_summary: Hebrew mitsvah, commandment — Leviticus 5:17; tsavah, to command — Deuteronomy 4:23; Greek koluo, to hinder or forbid — Acts 16:6.
roots_lines: Hebrew mitsvah — commandment; Leviticus 5:17, “the commandments of the LORD.”
Hebrew tsavah — to lay charge upon, command; Deuteronomy 4:23 of the graven image.
Greek koluo — to hinder, forbid, prevent; Acts 16:6, and Mark 10:14 of the children.
Greek eao — to permit, suffer; Acts 16:7, “the Spirit suffered them not.”
Old English forbeodan, to command against — the source of the English word.
usage: “Though he wist it not, yet is he guilty” — sins of ignorance are still sins.
“Forbidden of the Holy Ghost to preach the word in Asia” — a good thing, shut for a season.
“The Spirit suffered them not” — the second closed door, and then Troas.

pos: a. (apt to forget; used of the hearer who reads the law and walks away, and in the negative of the duty of hospitality)
etymology: From forget — Old English forgietan, from the privative for- and gietan, to get or grasp; to forget is to lose one's grip on a thing. The Greek at James 1:25 is epilesmone, forgetfulness; at Hebrews 13:2 the verb is epilanthanomai.
biblical_def: James uses the word for a specific and common failure: “But whoso looketh into the perfect law of liberty, and continueth therein, he being not a forgetful hearer, but a doer of the work, this man shall be blessed in his deed” (James 1:25). The verse follows the figure of the man who beholds his natural face in a glass, goes away, and straightway forgets what manner of man he was. That is the forgetful hearer — not a man who disagreed with the sermon but a man who agreed with it and walked out the door unchanged. James's remedy is not more information but continuance and doing: “be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves” (James 1:22). The writer to the Hebrews uses the negative of a duty easily let slip: “Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares” (Hebrews 13:2). Hospitality is not usually refused on principle; it is forgotten. And David commands his own soul against the same drift toward God's mercies: “Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits” (Psalm 103:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines forgetful as apt to forget, easily losing the remembrance of, and also inattentive or neglectful.
webster_full: FORGETFUL, a. Apt to forget; easily losing the remembrance of.
A forgetful man should use helps to strengthen his memory.
2. Heedless; careless; neglectful; inattentive.
Be not forgetful to entertain strangers. Heb. 13.
FORGETFULNESS, n. The quality of losing the remembrance of; oblivion; neglect.
scriptures: James 1:25
But whoso looketh into the perfect law of liberty, and continueth therein, he being not a forgetful hearer, but a doer of the work, this man shall be blessed in his deed.
James 1:22
But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.
Hebrews 13:2
Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.
Psalm 103:2
Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits:
corruption_summary: Hearing has been mistaken for obeying, so that a congregation well supplied with teaching can be entirely forgetful in James's sense.
corruption_paragraphs: Never in history has so much preaching been available to so many, and James's warning is aimed precisely at that situation. A man may listen to sermons continuously, agree with all of them, take notes, and be a forgetful hearer throughout — because the test James applies is not comprehension but continuance and doing. The mirror figure is exact: the man sees himself truly, and the seeing accomplishes nothing because he does not act on what he saw. Reformed congregations, which rightly prize careful teaching, are in the most danger here, since we are practised at evaluating a sermon and less practised at obeying one.

Hebrews 13:2 shows the ordinary shape of the failure. Almost nobody decides against hospitality; it simply does not get done, crowded out by a full week and a private house. The remedy in both texts is the same and it is unglamorous: continuance. James promises the blessing not to the hearer nor even to the doer in general but to the man who continueth therein and is blessed in his deed. David's method in Psalm 103 is worth copying — he addresses his own soul in the imperative and enumerates the benefits one at a time, because forgetting is the default and remembering must be deliberate.
roots_summary: Greek epilesmone, forgetfulness — James 1:25; epilanthanomai, to forget or neglect — Hebrews 13:2; Hebrew shakach, to forget — Psalm 103:2.
roots_lines: Greek epilesmone — forgetfulness; James 1:25, its only New Testament occurrence, literally “a hearer of forgetfulness.”
Greek epilanthanomai — to forget, to neglect; Hebrews 13:2 and 13:16.
Greek poietes — a doer, a maker; James 1:22 and 1:25, set against the mere hearer.
Hebrew shakach — to forget; Psalm 103:2, and repeatedly in Deuteronomy of forgetting the LORD.
Old English forgietan — to lose one's grasp of a thing; the privative for- plus gietan, to get.
usage: “Not a forgetful hearer, but a doer of the work” — the man in the mirror who walks away.
“Be not forgetful to entertain strangers” — hospitality is rarely refused, only forgotten.
“Forget not all his benefits” — David commanding his own soul to remember.
